claims.statement: Lexical coverage is positively related to L2 listening and viewing comprehension, but coverage predicts probabilities of comprehension rather than guaranteeing understanding.

For informal L2 listening, around 95% lexical coverage is a defensible candidate for relatively stable adequate comprehension, while performance around 90% shows greater between-learner variability; these figures are material- and criterion-dependent rather than universal thresholds.

In one direct short-documentary viewing experiment, approximately 95% lexical coverage supported an optimal adequate-comprehension criterion while substantially lower coverage could still support minimal content comprehension because imagery contributes meaning; this cannot be generalized into an independent-listening threshold.

Audiovisual imagery changes the comprehension construct: lexical coverage is more strongly tied to audio-dependent understanding than to information recoverable from imagery, so viewing comprehension and listening comprehension should not be treated as identical outcomes.

Large TV and movie corpora commonly reach about 95% lexical coverage around the 3,000-frequency/word-family region, while 98% requires substantially more vocabulary; genre, episode and methodological variation is large.

Corpus-wide vocabulary-size estimates cannot establish readiness for one specific authentic clip because local lexical demands vary; clip-specific lexical profiling is more appropriate for adaptive selection.
For audiovisual readiness, aural access to words/chunks is more relevant than orthographic familiarity alone because successful listening requires recognizing known language in speech.

Visual-semantic grounding can support comprehension and vocabulary learning; imagery that coincides closely with spoken referents is more pedagogically useful than unrelated or weakly informative visuals.

Beginner TV-viewing comprehension is influenced by prior vocabulary knowledge, lexical coverage and on-screen support; support can improve content comprehension without demonstrating independent listening.
Playback/speech rate interacts with captions and learner proficiency/listening ability; current evidence does not justify one universal words-per-minute threshold for authentic video readiness.
Authentic audiovisual input is best treated as gradable by local linguistic and multimodal properties rather than as a binary authentic-versus-graded category.

High overall token coverage can still mask a small number of unknown words that carry critical message content, so raw coverage percentage should be supplemented with the information value of unknown items.

Short source windows can in principle be pedagogically usable before an entire source becomes usable, but the optimal window duration and segmentation policy for Vietnamese near-A0 learners are not established by the literature.

The exact lexical-coverage bands, speech-load weights, visual-grounding thresholds and authentic-video unlock policy for Vietnamese near-A0 Nếp learners require direct validation and should not be presented as established scientific cutoffs.
